claims.question: q2
claims.claim: The docs recommend turning an interview into SPEC.md, starting a fresh session to build from it, and later pointing the reviewer at that file as the written definition of done.
claims.quote: Once `SPEC.md` exists, start a fresh session to build from it, so the build begins with a clean context and a written definition of done. It’s also the file you’ll point the reviewer at later, in [Give Claude a check to run](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices#give-claude-a-check-to-run).

claims.question: q2
claims.claim: CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session, so the docs advise keeping it to non-code-discoverable project facts rather than general guidance.
claims.quote: Claude Code loads [`CLAUDE.md`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) into every session, which means every line in it takes a little of Claude’s attention on _every_ task, whether it’s relevant or not. That’s why the file works best when it only holds what Claude couldn’t work out from the code itself:

claims.quote: That kind of knowledge goes in a [skill](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills): a procedure or a piece of team knowledge saved at `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: Docs name a common failure mode where Claude reports completion even though the work is not done because it could not check its own work.
claims.quote: Claude said it was done and it wasn’t quite, usually because it had no way to check its own work.

claims.question: q5
claims.claim: Prompt, CLAUDE.md, and skills are non-deterministic because the model decides whether to follow them; there is no guarantee.
claims.quote: Non-deterministic: you write the instruction, and Claude (the model) reads it. This can be your prompt, `CLAUDE.md`, or a skill. The model then decides what to do with this information. It usually follows your commands, and current models are good at understanding your intent without much context, but there’s no _guarantee_ that it’ll follow your instructions.
